chapter.title: Adding the arms

cards.body: The breath you take while swimming works backwards from the one you take on land, and today your arms will show you why. You're still lying on the same bed of water. Now **one arm rests out on the pillow ahead of you while the other sweeps back underneath**, then they swap.
cards.simpler: Breathing while swimming works the opposite way from breathing on land, and today your arms will show you why. Picture yourself still lying on the same bed of water. Now **one arm rests out on the pillow ahead of you while the other sweeps back underneath**. Then they swap places.

cards.prompt: You've pushed off and you're gliding, face down, both arms out front. Your right arm starts its pull. What should your left arm be doing?

options.text: Pulling at the same time, for double the push
Staying stretched out front, resting on the water
Tucked by your side to make you thinner

whyNot.a: That's chasing power, not balance: with both arms back at once, nothing is holding the front of you up on the bed.
whyNot.c: That's a torpedo shape, not a stroke: with no arm out front, your chest presses down and your legs start to sink.

cards.reteach: Picture your front arm as the pillow under your head. Take the pillow away and your head drops, then your legs follow. So one arm always waits out front while the other one works.

cards.title: Arms take turns
cards.body:
Front crawl arms take turns. One arm reaches forward and pulls back under your body, all the way to your thigh. Then it lifts out, elbow first, and swings forward over the water. That swing is the *recovery*, meaning the arm's ride back through the air.

Meanwhile **the other arm waits, stretched out flat on the water**, like a hand resting on a kitchen table. It stays there until the working hand nearly touches it. Coaches call this *catch-up*.

Practise standing first: chest-deep, lean forward, face in. Your pulling hand should brush past your belly button, not swing out wide like a gate.
cards.simpler: Front crawl arms take turns. One arm reaches forward, pulls back under your body to your thigh, then lifts out elbow first and swings forward over the water. Meanwhile **the other arm waits, stretched flat on the water**, like a hand resting on a kitchen table, until the working hand nearly touches it. Coaches call this catch-up. Practise standing chest-deep first: lean forward, face in. Your pulling hand should brush your belly button, not swing wide like a gate.

cards.title: Dev's fourth stroke
cards.body: Dev, 34, tries it in the shallow end before work. Standing up, it feels almost silly. From a push-off he does 3 slow catch-up strokes with his face in, and stands up past the spot where his glide used to run out. Then he goes for 6. By stroke 4 he's speeding up, arms spinning like a paddle steamer, legs sinking, and he stands up gasping. His arms didn't get tired in two strokes. **He'd been holding his breath since the wall.**
cards.simpler: Dev, 34, tries this in the shallow end before work. Standing up, it feels almost silly. He pushes off and does 3 slow catch-up strokes with his face in, and stands up past where his glide used to stop. Then he tries 6. By stroke 4 he's speeding up, arms spinning like a paddle steamer, legs sinking. He stands up gasping. His arms didn't get tired in two strokes. **He'd been holding his breath since the wall.**

cards.prompt: Amara swims 3 lovely strokes, but by stroke 5 her arms are whirling and her legs drop. What should she change on her next try?

options.text: Kick much harder to hold her legs up
Slow down so one hand waits out front until the other catches up, breathing out the whole way
Lift her head to keep the far wall in sight

whyNot.a: That's chapter 5's trap, not the fix: a bigger kick moves you less, and it still leaves no arm out front.
whyNot.c: That's a balance breaker, not a fix: lifting your head pushes your hips and legs further down.

cards.reteach: Whirling arms mean no arm is out front, so the bed tips and your legs sink. Slowing down puts a hand back on the pillow. A steady out-breath stops the rush that makes you whirl in the first place.

cards.title: Breathing backwards
cards.body:
On land you breathe in on purpose and let the air fall out by itself. Swimming flips that around. **Breathe out slowly the whole time your face is in**, through your nose and mouth, then take one quick breath in when you stand.

Hold your breath instead and it starts to feel like a countdown, so you rush. By stroke 5, your body is shouting for fresh air.

Aim for a trickle, like a kettle on low, not a balloon popping. A trickle leaves air in your chest, and that air keeps you up on the bed. Do 3 strokes with bubbles all the way, then try 6.
cards.simpler: On land you breathe in on purpose and let air fall out. Swimming flips that. **Breathe out slowly the whole time your face is in**, through nose and mouth, then breathe in quickly when you stand. Holding your breath feels like a countdown, so you rush and need air by stroke 5. Aim for a trickle, like a kettle on low, not a popping balloon. Leftover air keeps you floating. Try 3 strokes bubbling all the way, then 6.

cards.body: Sam pushes off and swims like he's late for a bus: arms windmilling, breath clamped shut, lots of splash. He gets about 5 metres and stands up red-faced, sure his arms are weak. **The easy check: if you can't remember feeling one hand resting out front, you went too fast.** No rest out front means no bubbles either.
cards.simpler: Sam pushes off and swims like he's late for a bus: arms windmilling, breath held tight, lots of splashing. He gets about 5 metres, stands up red-faced, and decides his arms are weak. **Here's the easy check: if you can't remember feeling one hand resting out front, you went too fast.** And no rest out front means no breathing out either.

cards.prompt: Your friend asks what good beginner front crawl arms look like. Which answer do you give?

options.text: Keep both arms spinning so there's never a gap
One arm rests out front while the other pulls under you and swings over, with a slow breath out the whole time
Let the arms do the work so the legs can stop kicking

whyNot.a: That's the windmill, not the stroke: with no arm out front you lose your bed and rush your breath.
whyNot.c: That's swapping one move for another, not adding one: the arms go on top of the kick, they don't replace it.

cards.reteach: Crawl is slow turn-taking: one hand waits on the water, the other pulls back to your thigh and swings forward to meet it. Bubbles go out the whole time. That's what makes 6 strokes feel easy instead of frantic.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Front crawl arms take turns: **one rests out front on the water while the other pulls back under your body and swings over the top**. Go slowly, breathe out the whole time your face is in, and 6 strokes feel calm instead of frantic.

Tomorrow: why your back, not the wall, is the safest place to rest.
cards.simpler: Front crawl arms take turns: **one rests out front on the water while the other pulls back under your body and swings over the top**. Go slowly and breathe out the whole time your face is in. Do that, and 6 strokes feel calm instead of frantic. Tomorrow: why your back, not the wall, is the safest place to rest.

cards.body: Tonight at home: bend forward at a table with one hand resting on it. Pull the other arm back past your thigh, swing it over, and touch the first hand. Swap. Do 6 strokes, humming out the whole time.
cards.simpler: Tonight at home, bend forward over a table and rest one hand on it. Pull your other arm back past your thigh, swing it over the top, and touch the first hand. Then swap. Do 6 strokes, and **hum out the whole time**, so you get used to breathing out while your arms move.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now swim 6 to 8 slow front crawl strokes from a push-off, one hand waiting out front and breathing out the whole way, then stand up calmly.
